Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. This, coupled with the area's lack of green space, makes Downtown Brooklyn most appealing to those who can embrace one of Brooklyn's busiest and most trafficked neighborhoods. Its appeal and vibrancy stem from its housing stock. Handsome Greek revival and Italianate townhouses line the wide, tree-lined streets. These beautiful brick and limestone buildings have long been a mecca for Brooklynites seeking an enclave close to Downtown Brooklyn and lower Manhattan — but far from crowds and highrises. Main drags like Bergen Street, Atlantic Avenue, and Smith Street are peppered with charming boutiques like Collier West in addition to welcoming cafes, bars, and restaurants, including Rucola, French Louie, and Bacchus, to name a few. Fans of new construction will find new condo developments too. Saint Marks Place, The Hendrick, The Boerum, and The Bergen have expanded buyers' opportunities. Renters will also find plenty of options here in a broad range of prices, from the genuinely affordable to the luxurious. Sales Median asking price 1 bed $950K Rentals Median asking base rent 1 bed $4,325 Energetic and inviting, Boerum Hill continues its run as one of New York City's most desirable neighborhoods, all while remaining a secret quietly shared amongst its happy residents. Its appeal and vibrancy stem from its housing stock. Handsome Greek revival and Italianate townhouses line the wide, tree-lined streets. These beautiful brick and limestone buildings have long been a mecca for Brooklynites seeking an enclave close to Downtown Brooklyn and lower Manhattan — but far from crowds and highrises. Main drags like Bergen Street, Atlantic Avenue, and Smith Street are peppered with charming boutiques like Collier West in addition to welcoming cafes, bars, and restaurants, including Rucola, French Louie, and Bacchus, to name a few. Fans of new construction will find new condo developments too. Saint Marks Place, The Hendrick, The Boerum, and The Bergen have expanded buyers' opportunities. Renters will also find plenty of options here in a broad range of prices, from the genuinely affordable to the luxurious. Its appeal and vibrancy stem from its housing stock. Handsome Greek revival and Italianate townhouses line the wide, tree-lined streets. Sales Median asking price 1 bed $699K Rentals Median asking base rent 1 bed $3,895 When George Washington commandeered the building site that would eventually become Gracie Mansion, he probably didn't imagine that this peaceful, riverside enclave would become the lively residential neighborhood it is today. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Sales Median asking price 1 bed $950K Rentals Median asking base rent 1 bed $4,325 Energetic and inviting, Boerum Hill continues its run as one of New York City's most desirable neighborhoods, all while remaining a secret quietly shared amongst its happy residents. Its appeal and vibrancy stem from its housing stock. Handsome Greek revival and Italianate townhouses line the wide, tree-lined streets. These beautiful brick and limestone buildings have long been a mecca for Brooklynites seeking an enclave close to Downtown Brooklyn and lower Manhattan — but far from crowds and highrises. Main drags like Bergen Street, Atlantic Avenue, and Smith Street are peppered with charming boutiques like Collier West in addition to welcoming cafes, bars, and restaurants, including Rucola, French Louie, and Bacchus, to name a few. Fans of new construction will find new condo developments too. Saint Marks Place, The Hendrick, The Boerum, and The Bergen have expanded buyers' opportunities. Renters will also find plenty of options here in a broad range of prices, from the genuinely affordable to the luxurious. Energetic and inviting, Boerum Hill continues its run as one of New York City's most desirable neighborhoods, all while remaining a secret quietly shared amongst its happy residents. Its appeal and vibrancy stem from its housing stock. Handsome Greek revival and Italianate townhouses line the wide, tree-lined streets. These beautiful brick and limestone buildings have long been a mecca for Brooklynites seeking an enclave close to Downtown Brooklyn and lower Manhattan — but far from crowds and highrises. Main drags like Bergen Street, Atlantic Avenue, and Smith Street are peppered with charming boutiques like Collier West in addition to welcoming cafes, bars, and restaurants, including Rucola, French Louie, and Bacchus, to name a few. Fans of new construction will find new condo developments too. Saint Marks Place, The Hendrick, The Boerum, and The Bergen have expanded buyers' opportunities. Renters will also find plenty of options here in a broad range of prices, from the genuinely affordable to the luxurious. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Despite the abundance of seven-figure homes, Cobble Hill has small-town vibe evident in the mom-and-pop stores and Italian influences that dot Court Street. Walk down the sunny commercial strip and you'll pass the local butcher, the baker and the fishmonger — all family-run and equally popular among local residents and foodies from far and wide. Log in Explore Yorkville TRANSIT SCHOOLS COLLEGES PARKS MUSEUMS Transit Location Distance Qat 86th St 0.12 miles 6at 77th St 0.35 miles 456at 86th St 0.36 miles Qat 72nd St 0.48 miles Qat 96th St 0.64 miles View transit on Google Maps View on Google Maps About Yorkville Sales Median asking price 2 beds $1.33M Rentals Median asking base rent 2 beds $4,950 When George Washington commandeered the building site that would eventually become Gracie Mansion, he probably didn't imagine that this peaceful, riverside enclave would become the lively residential neighborhood it is today. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Its appeal and vibrancy stem from its housing stock. Handsome Greek revival and Italianate townhouses line the wide, tree-lined streets. These beautiful brick and limestone buildings have long been a mecca for Brooklynites seeking an enclave close to Downtown Brooklyn and lower Manhattan — but far from crowds and highrises. Main drags like Bergen Street, Atlantic Avenue, and Smith Street are peppered with charming boutiques like Collier West in addition to welcoming cafes, bars, and restaurants, including Rucola, French Louie, and Bacchus, to name a few. Fans of new construction will find new condo developments too. Saint Marks Place, The Hendrick, The Boerum, and The Bergen have expanded buyers' opportunities. Renters will also find plenty of options here in a broad range of prices, from the genuinely affordable to the luxurious. Its appeal and vibrancy stem from its housing stock. Handsome Greek revival and Italianate townhouses line the wide, tree-lined streets. These beautiful brick and limestone buildings have long been a mecca for Brooklynites seeking an enclave close to Downtown Brooklyn and lower Manhattan — but far from crowds and highrises. Fans of new construction will find new condo developments too. Saint Marks Place, The Hendrick, The Boerum, and The Bergen have expanded buyers' opportunities. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. listing.description:
Rarely Available — This Prospect Heights pre-war one-bedroom garden apartment with private outdoor access is now on the market to rent.

Sunny and expansive, this home offers a flexible layout, with a separate mud area, entrance hall, spacious living area, and direct access to the backyard. A private entrance provides convenience for bike storage, and the apartment includes basement storage and laundry.

The generously sized living room features hardwood flooring, an original marble fireplace, and plenty of space for separate living and dining areas. listing.description: Available September 1 21 Butler Place #3D - Prospect Heights Welcome home to this beautifully renovated one-bedroom, one-bath residence nestled on a quiet, tree-lined block in the heart of Prospect Heights. Apartment 3D perfectly blends classic Brooklyn charm with modern finishes, creating a warm and inviting place to call home. The thoughtfully updated apartment features an open chef's kitchen complete with stainless steel appliances, including a dishwasher, quartz countertops, abundant cabinetry, and a pantry for exceptional storage. The inviting living room is highlighted by custom designer wallpaper, adding warmth and character to the space. The spacious bedroom easily accommodates a queen- or king-sized bed and features a generous double closet. Both the living room and bedroom are equipped with built-in ceiling fans and recessed LED lighting, providing year-round comfort and a modern aesthetic. The windowed bathroom has been tastefully renovated with sleek, contemporary tilework and stylish finishes. Residents enjoy an excellent collection of building amenities, including a common roof deck with sweeping neighborhood views, a laundry room, bike storage, and a live-in superintendent. Located just moments from Prospect Park, Grand Army Plaza, the Brooklyn Museum, the Brooklyn Botanic Garden, and the Brooklyn Public Library, this home places you in the center of one of Brooklyn's most vibrant neighborhoods. Enjoy easy access to the 2, 3, B, and Q subway lines, while the renowned restaurants, cafés, boutiques, and nightlife along Vanderbilt and Washington Avenues are only a short stroll away. Pets are welcome upon approval. Don't miss this opportunity to live in one of Brooklyn's most desirable neighborhoods.

listing.description:
Paseo on Fifth is a vibrant new residential development in the heart of Park Slope, Brooklyn. Nestled within The Paseo—a thoughtfully designed pedestrian passage where Fifth Avenue meets Sterling Place—this one-of-a-kind address offers a peaceful retreat amid the energy of the neighborhood. Framed by curated retail and local charm, The Paseo fosters a unique sense of community and calm just steps from home.

Enter the exquisite residences at Paseo on Fifth, where sophisticated design meets modern practicality. From airy studios to expansive two-bedroom apartments, explore a range of layouts with luxurious finishes to enhance your daily living. Residences feature up to 10’ 9” ceiling heights, wide plank flooring in a light oak finish, and floor-to-ceiling windows that flood interiors with natural light. Quartz countertops, custom tile work, and Kohler fixtures with rainfall showerheads elevate kitchens and baths with refined detail, while stainless steel appliances from Bosch and Samsung add modern functionality.

At Paseo on Fifth, you will find an amenities suite that truly harmonizes with your daily rhythm. Dive into a meticulously designed environment where everything from the cutting-edge gym and yoga studio to the plush coworking spaces transforms everyday tasks into elements of a curated lifestyle. Seamlessly transition from productivity in our high-tech workspaces to relaxation in The Hub, each space crafted with a keen eye for function and style.

• Virtual Doorman
• Rooftop Garden
• Lobby Lounge
• Coworking Lounge
• The Library
• Second Floor Terrace
• Crafts Studio
• Smart Package Room
• Bike Storage
• Laundry Convenience
• Storage
• Valet Parking

Application Fee: $20 per person
Security Deposit: 1 month’s rent
Amenities Fee: $50/month per tenant
Storage: $50 - $75/month
Bike Storage: $15/Month per bike
Pet Fee: $25/month per pet
Utilities: Rent includes hot water and sewage; residents cover electricity, cable, and internet.

Marketed by Compass Development Marketing Group.

listing.title: Kips Bay studio asks $499K
listing.bodyText: Skip main navigation Search NYC Apartments Reads Search NYC Apartments Good Deals Deal of the Week Most Popular Open Houses Sales Deals Rental Deals Renting NYC Renters' Rights: Resource Hub for Renters NYC Renters' Guide Housing Lotteries Tips and Advice for Renters Buying & Selling Working With a Buyer's Agent: Resource Hub for Buyers First-Time Buyer Guide Buyer Tips and Advice Selling Your Home NYC Life Neighborhood Guides NYC Moving Guide Celebrity Homes Market Data Data Dashboard Market Reports Neighborhood Data Affordability Industry Hub Latest Industry Standards: Resource Hub for Agents Deal of the Week Kips Bay studio asks $499K By Erika Riley Sep. 1, 2026 If you’re looking to live near Midtown but don’t want to constantly be in the hustle and bustle, consider Kips Bay. This Midtown East enclave feels residential and laid-back while offering easy access to the rest of Manhattan. Plus, its low profile comes with prices a bit lower than borough averages. Our Deal of the Week is 305 E. 24th St. #14K, a Kips Bay studio in a full-service building. While you’re at it, check out StreetEasy’s new Neighborhood Guide to Kips Bay. 305 E. 24th St. #14K Price $499,000 Space Studio, 1 bath Neighborhood Kips Bay Borough Manhattan Get to know our Deal of the Week. View Listing The price: $499,000 The median asking price for a home in Midtown East was $900,000 this July, according to the StreetEasy Data Dashboard. That means our Deal of the Week is priced a little above half the median asking price for the greater neighborhood! Buyers who put down a 20% down payment of $99,800 can expect to see monthly payments of $3,663. This includes a mortgage payment of $2,507 and maintenance fees of $1,156. Monthly payments sit well below the median asking rent in Midtown East, which was $5,100 this July. Why you’ll love it… Many New York City studios are short on closet space, but not this one. You’ll find a wall of closets in the dining area, plus a smaller one outside the kitchen that could be used as a pantry. There’s even a dressing area connecting the main living area to the bathroom, with built-in storage and yet another closet. Another common studio struggle is a tiny kitchen placed in the same room as everything else. But never fear: this unit has its own separate U-shaped kitchen complete with full-size appliances — no mini-fridge here. Among these appliances are a mounted microwave and a dishwasher for ultimate convenience. There’s lots of storage in this room as well thanks to custom cabinetry. Tile backsplash and granite countertops bring the room together. The main room of this studio has enough space for a bed, couch, desk, and dining table. It’s also filled with light thanks to three east-facing windows. Lastly, the unit’s bathroom has a shower/tub combo with a glass sliding door, a vanity with storage, and recessed lighting. To top it all off, the apartment has central air conditioning. The unit is located on a high floor of a full-service elevator building with a 24-hour attended lobby. Amenities include a package room, concierge services, laundry facilities, bike storage, and extra storage. On-site parking with valet is available for $350 per month. Co-purchasing and pied-à-terres are permitted, and subletting is allowed every two years out of four. Located in Kips Bay, the building is near the 6, R, W, and L trains in addition to several bus lines. Buyers will have a slew of parks close by, including Bellevue South Park, Madison Square Park, and Stuyvesant Square. There’s also a Trader Joe’s just a few blocks north. …and why you might not The windows in the living area are the only ones in the unit — both the kitchen and bathroom are window-less. The building is right near several hospitals, which is great for healthcare workers, but not so great for those looking to avoid the sound of ambulances. But for less than $500K, so many amenities, and a generous amount of space for a studio, this one is not to be missed! Check out the listing at 305 E. 24th St. #14K, listed by Josue Gonzalez and Brooklyn Miller of Coldwell Banker Warburg. Buying a home in NYC is unlike buying anywhere else. listing.description:
Welcome to this renovated and versatile Park Slope home, originally configured as a one-bedroom and thoughtfully converted to provide two other extra separate areas, creating valuable flexibility for today’s lifestyle.

The apartment features beautiful hardwood floors, a spacious living area, and a renovated contemporary kitchen with white cabinetry, quartz-style countertops, subway-tile backsplash, and stainless-steel appliances, including a gas range, dishwasher, and full-size refrigerator. Generous counter space and a breakfast bar make the kitchen both functional and inviting.

The renovated bathroom offers a clean, modern aesthetic with a glass-enclosed shower, subway tile, contemporary vanity, and tiled flooring. Adding tremendous convenience is an in-unit washer and dryer.

The flexible layout includes a generously sized primary bedroom with closet storage, plus a second room that can function as a bedroom, an extra home office, a nursery, guest room, or additional living space. Split-system heating and air conditioning provide year-round comfort.

The location is another major highlight. The apartment is conveniently located near the 4th Avenue–9th Street subway station, with F, G, and R train service, providing easy access to Manhattan and neighborhoods throughout Brooklyn.

Enjoy the best of the Park Slope lifestyle, with Fifth Avenue’s excellent selection of restaurants, cafés, bars, shops, and neighborhood conveniences just a short distance away. The area offers everything from casual neighborhood favorites and coffee shops to destination dining, along with easy access to the many amenities that make Park Slope one of Brooklyn’s most desirable neighborhoods.

With its renovated interiors, flexible two-to-three extra room configuration, in-unit laundry, air conditioning, private entrance, excellent transportation, and prime Park Slope location, this apartment offers an appealing combination of comfort, convenience, and value. Plus located in the area of School District 15.

listing.description:
∗∗ The Landmark – Park Slope ∗ Spacious, 2BD/2BA with Floor-To-Ceiling Windows, Gourmet Kitchen with Stainless Steel Appliances, Washer/Dryer in a Luxury Doorman Building with Roof Deck, Lounge, and Fitness Center ∗∗

Welcome to The Landmark. These homes reflect a contemporary way of life and have been designed to accommodate discerning lifestyles. Each apartment has been planned with a gracious eye and fitted with top quality finishes including floor-to-ceiling windows in the large living rooms, hardwood floors throughout, and spacious bathrooms. The gourmet Chefs kitchen boasts sprawling counters and tons of cabinets, stainless steel appliances, microwave, and dishwasher. Nearly every home features sweeping views and in-unit washer/dryers.

Building amenities include a doorman and concierge, roof deck with stunning views, residents lounge, and fitness center. Conveniently located near transportation with the R, F and G trains just down the street. Surrounded by restaurants, coffee shops, a farmers market, shopping, nightlife, and even a Whole Foods around the corner! Photos are of a similar unit in the building.

This apartment can be rented deposit free. Pay a small monthly fee to Rhino, and never pay a security deposit again. Please ask the leasing agent for more information.


**Pursuant to the Fairness in Apartment Rental Expenses (FARE) Act and the Fair Housing Act, we are required to disclose all fees associated with the rental process.
A comprehensive list of fees will be disclosed prior to lease signing in the form of a Tenant Fee Disclosure form and will include and is not limited to the following:
Application Fee: $20 per leaseholder/guarantor
Security Deposit: Equal to 1 month’s rent
First Month’s rent: Equal to First Month’s rent **

Sales Median asking price 1 bed $899K Rentals Median asking base rent 1 bed $4,100 When many people think of the Upper East Side, they think of a quiet, tree-lined urban expanse filled with posh residents and purebred dogs. There's some reality behind the neighborhood's old-money image: The blocks between Park and Fifth avenues are home to some of Manhattan's wealthiest residents, many of whom dwell in stately co-ops or sleek new condos overseen by stiffly collared doormen. But there's a lot more happening on the Upper East Side. Museum Mile throngs with tourists, street artists, and lovers of the arts, drawn to its abundance of high culture. And the eastern side of the neighborhood, toward Yorkville, exhibits a less rarefied character. Second Avenue is home to sports bars, pubs, and some excellent restaurants. A trendy renaissance is in the offing here, sparked by young professionals drawn by some surprisingly good housing prices (for Manhattan). The avenues and commerce-lined thoroughfares can be hectic, but many streets on the Upper East Side are blessedly quiet — just one more way in which this oft-stereotyped neighborhood can be a surprise. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Sun-Drenched Two-Bedroom on Vanderbilt Avenue — Prospect Heights

Freshly renovated and ready for move-in, this spacious floor-through two-bedroom, one-bath apartment offers the best of Prospect Heights living — polished, comfortable, and perfectly placed just steps from Vanderbilt Avenue’s beloved restaurant row and boutique shops.
Set on the second floor of a classic Brooklyn brick building, the home features good ceiling height, exposed brick, and rich hardwood floors throughout, all bathed in abundant natural light.
The newly updated kitchen and bath bring a modern touch to the space’s timeless character, while a cozy nook offers the ideal setup for a home office or reading corner. An in-unit washer/dryer combo adds everyday convenience rarely found at this price point.

Just moments from Prospect Park, residents enjoy easy access to the Long Meadow, the Boathouse, and the weekend Grand Army Plaza Greenmarket — a rare blend of green space and city energy right outside your door. Commuting is effortless with the 2/3, B/Q, and Franklin Ave Shuttle all nearby, putting Manhattan within easy reach.

Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. There's some reality behind the neighborhood's old-money image: The blocks between Park and Fifth avenues are home to some of Manhattan's wealthiest residents, many of whom dwell in stately co-ops or sleek new condos overseen by stiffly collared doormen. But there's a lot more happening on the Upper East Side. Museum Mile throngs with tourists, street artists, and lovers of the arts, drawn to its abundance of high culture. And the eastern side of the neighborhood, toward Yorkville, exhibits a less rarefied character. Second Avenue is home to sports bars, pubs, and some excellent restaurants. A trendy renaissance is in the offing here, sparked by young professionals drawn by some surprisingly good housing prices (for Manhattan). The avenues and commerce-lined thoroughfares can be hectic, but many streets on the Upper East Side are blessedly quiet — just one more way in which this oft-stereotyped neighborhood can be a surprise. There's some reality behind the neighborhood's old-money image: The blocks between Park and Fifth avenues are home to some of Manhattan's wealthiest residents, many of whom dwell in stately co-ops or sleek new condos overseen by stiffly collared doormen. Sales Median asking price 1 bed $699K Rentals Median asking base rent 1 bed $3,895 When George Washington commandeered the building site that would eventually become Gracie Mansion, he probably didn't imagine that this peaceful, riverside enclave would become the lively residential neighborhood it is today. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Its appeal and vibrancy stem from its housing stock. Handsome Greek revival and Italianate townhouses line the wide, tree-lined streets. These beautiful brick and limestone buildings have long been a mecca for Brooklynites seeking an enclave close to Downtown Brooklyn and lower Manhattan — but far from crowds and highrises. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. Its appeal and vibrancy stem from its housing stock. Handsome Greek revival and Italianate townhouses line the wide, tree-lined streets. These beautiful brick and limestone buildings have long been a mecca for Brooklynites seeking an enclave close to Downtown Brooklyn and lower Manhattan — but far from crowds and highrises. Main drags like Bergen Street, Atlantic Avenue, and Smith Street are peppered with charming boutiques like Collier West in addition to welcoming cafes, bars, and restaurants, including Rucola, French Louie, and Bacchus, to name a few. Fans of new construction will find new condo developments too. Saint Marks Place, The Hendrick, The Boerum, and The Bergen have expanded buyers' opportunities. Renters will also find plenty of options here in a broad range of prices, from the genuinely affordable to the luxurious. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Its appeal and vibrancy stem from its housing stock. Handsome Greek revival and Italianate townhouses line the wide, tree-lined streets. These beautiful brick and limestone buildings have long been a mecca for Brooklynites seeking an enclave close to Downtown Brooklyn and lower Manhattan — but far from crowds and highrises. Main drags like Bergen Street, Atlantic Avenue, and Smith Street are peppered with charming boutiques like Collier West in addition to welcoming cafes, bars, and restaurants, including Rucola, French Louie, and Bacchus, to name a few. Fans of new construction will find new condo developments too. Saint Marks Place, The Hendrick, The Boerum, and The Bergen have expanded buyers' opportunities. Renters will also find plenty of options here in a broad range of prices, from the genuinely affordable to the luxurious. Its appeal and vibrancy stem from its housing stock. Handsome Greek revival and Italianate townhouses line the wide, tree-lined streets. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. From the chaotic, commercial avenues of Nostrand and Utica to the wide, tree-lined esplanades of Eastern Parkway, the streets are always filled with locals shopping, catching up on the corner, and keeping tabs on neighbors. Walk down any of these streets and you're likely to find music playing from idling cars and bright Caribbean flags hanging from windows of apartment buildings. Every Labor Day, Crown Heights hosts the West Indian Day Parade, one of the city's largest annual street festivals which draws thousands of people from around the city and the world. The mix of people in such close proximity makes Crown Heights a fascinating microcosm of New York City. Living here, you'll be surrounded by a community with deep roots and rich heritage. From the chaotic, commercial avenues of Nostrand and Utica to the wide, tree-lined esplanades of Eastern Parkway, the streets are always filled with locals shopping, catching up on the corner, and keeping tabs on neighbors. Walk down any of these streets and you're likely to find music playing from idling cars and bright Caribbean flags hanging from windows of apartment buildings. Every Labor Day, Crown Heights hosts the West Indian Day Parade, one of the city's largest annual street festivals which draws thousands of people from around the city and the world. The mix of people in such close proximity makes Crown Heights a fascinating microcosm of New York City. Living here, you'll be surrounded by a community with deep roots and rich heritage. From the chaotic, commercial avenues of Nostrand and Utica to the wide, tree-lined esplanades of Eastern Parkway, the streets are always filled with locals shopping, catching up on the corner, and keeping tabs on neighbors. Walk down any of these streets and you're likely to find music playing from idling cars and bright Caribbean flags hanging from windows of apartment buildings. Every Labor Day, Crown Heights hosts the West Indian Day Parade, one of the city's largest annual street festivals which draws thousands of people from around the city and the world. Its appeal and vibrancy stem from its housing stock. Handsome Greek revival and Italianate townhouses line the wide, tree-lined streets. Its appeal and vibrancy stem from its housing stock. Handsome Greek revival and Italianate townhouses line the wide, tree-lined streets. These beautiful brick and limestone buildings have long been a mecca for Brooklynites seeking an enclave close to Downtown Brooklyn and lower Manhattan — but far from crowds and highrises. Main drags like Bergen Street, Atlantic Avenue, and Smith Street are peppered with charming boutiques like Collier West in addition to welcoming cafes, bars, and restaurants, including Rucola, French Louie, and Bacchus, to name a few. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Its appeal and vibrancy stem from its housing stock. Handsome Greek revival and Italianate townhouses line the wide, tree-lined streets. These beautiful brick and limestone buildings have long been a mecca for Brooklynites seeking an enclave close to Downtown Brooklyn and lower Manhattan — but far from crowds and highrises. Main drags like Bergen Street, Atlantic Avenue, and Smith Street are peppered with charming boutiques like Collier West in addition to welcoming cafes, bars, and restaurants, including Rucola, French Louie, and Bacchus, to name a few. Fans of new construction will find new condo developments too. Saint Marks Place, The Hendrick, The Boerum, and The Bergen have expanded buyers' opportunities. Renters will also find plenty of options here in a broad range of prices, from the genuinely affordable to the luxurious. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Its appeal and vibrancy stem from its housing stock. Handsome Greek revival and Italianate townhouses line the wide, tree-lined streets. These beautiful brick and limestone buildings have long been a mecca for Brooklynites seeking an enclave close to Downtown Brooklyn and lower Manhattan — but far from crowds and highrises. Main drags like Bergen Street, Atlantic Avenue, and Smith Street are peppered with charming boutiques like Collier West in addition to welcoming cafes, bars, and restaurants, including Rucola, French Louie, and Bacchus, to name a few. Fans of new construction will find new condo developments too. Saint Marks Place, The Hendrick, The Boerum, and The Bergen have expanded buyers' opportunities. Its appeal and vibrancy stem from its housing stock. Handsome Greek revival and Italianate townhouses line the wide, tree-lined streets. Main drags like Bergen Street, Atlantic Avenue, and Smith Street are peppered with charming boutiques like Collier West in addition to welcoming cafes, bars, and restaurants, including Rucola, French Louie, and Bacchus, to name a few. Fans of new construction will find new condo developments too. Saint Marks Place, The Hendrick, The Boerum, and The Bergen have expanded buyers' opportunities. Renters will also find plenty of options here in a broad range of prices, from the genuinely affordable to the luxurious. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. listing.description:
Two-bedroom parlor-floor condominium in the heart of Prospect Heights,

This home offers the perfect combination of classic Brooklyn character and modern comfort. Set within a charming pre-war building on a picturesque tree-lined street, this inviting two-bedroom home features SOARING CEILINGS, BEAUTIFUL NATURAL LIGHT, AND ORIGINAL PRE-WAR DETAILS that give the space warmth and personality. The thoughtfully designed layout offers two bedrooms, comfortable living space, and built-in closets providing generous storage. The parlor-floor setting and high ceilings create an airy, residential feel, while the renovated interiors offer the ease and comfort of modern living. The location is hard to beat. Just moments from PROSPECT PARK AND GRAND ARMY PLAZA, you'll have some of Brooklyn's best green space, dining, shopping, cafés, and cultural destinations right outside your door. Getting around the city is equally convenient, with the 2/3 and B/Q subway lines nearby, providing easy access throughout Brooklyn and into Manhattan.

listing.description:
532 10th Street is a boutique 5-unit building tucked away on a quiet, residential street in the heart of Park Slope offering recently renovated units that showcase a thoughtful blend between pre-war charm and modern-day conveniences.

Apartment 2 is a well-proportioned 1-bed 1-bath boasting an abundance of natural light through two exposures and windows in every room. Enjoy 9' ceiling heights and original pre-war moldings while experiencing the luxury of modern upgrades like central AC/heating from a ductless mini split air system. 

The windowed, eat-in kitchen also features stainless steel appliances, including a dishwasher and microwave, as well as a combo washer/dryer for ultimate convenience. The spacious bedroom easily fits a queen-sized bed, plus furniture, and overlooks 10th street, a quiet townhouse lined block.

532 10th Street is surrounded by some of Park Slope's best restaurants and shopping – the building is also only a short walk from Prospect Park and a stone's throw from various subway lines, including the F at 7th-Ave and the G/R at 9th-Street for seamless commuting into the city.

There's some reality behind the neighborhood's old-money image: The blocks between Park and Fifth avenues are home to some of Manhattan's wealthiest residents, many of whom dwell in stately co-ops or sleek new condos overseen by stiffly collared doormen. But there's a lot more happening on the Upper East Side. Museum Mile throngs with tourists, street artists, and lovers of the arts, drawn to its abundance of high culture. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. There's some reality behind the neighborhood's old-money image: The blocks between Park and Fifth avenues are home to some of Manhattan's wealthiest residents, many of whom dwell in stately co-ops or sleek new condos overseen by stiffly collared doormen. But there's a lot more happening on the Upper East Side. Museum Mile throngs with tourists, street artists, and lovers of the arts, drawn to its abundance of high culture. And the eastern side of the neighborhood, toward Yorkville, exhibits a less rarefied character. Second Avenue is home to sports bars, pubs, and some excellent restaurants. The avenues and commerce-lined thoroughfares can be hectic, but many streets on the Upper East Side are blessedly quiet — just one more way in which this oft-stereotyped neighborhood can be a surprise. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. Despite the abundance of seven-figure homes, Cobble Hill has small-town vibe evident in the mom-and-pop stores and Italian influences that dot Court Street. Walk down the sunny commercial strip and you'll pass the local butcher, the baker and the fishmonger — all family-run and equally popular among local residents and foodies from far and wide. On the side streets, the homes tend to be large brick townhouses and brownstones owned by single families, with well-kept facades and window boxes. This is a neighborhood where homeownership is a luxury, and residents take that responsibility to heart. The blocks are clean, the community associations active, and the lifestyle warm and genteel. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Log in Explore Upper East Side TRANSIT SCHOOLS COLLEGES PARKS MUSEUMS Transit Location Distance 6at 77th St 0.22 miles 456at 86th St 0.23 miles Qat 86th St 0.24 miles Qat 72nd St 0.52 miles Qat 96th St 0.66 miles View transit on Google Maps View on Google Maps About Upper East Side Sales Median asking price 3 beds $3.95M Rentals Median asking base rent 3 beds $15,150 When many people think of the Upper East Side, they think of a quiet, tree-lined urban expanse filled with posh residents and purebred dogs. There's some reality behind the neighborhood's old-money image: The blocks between Park and Fifth avenues are home to some of Manhattan's wealthiest residents, many of whom dwell in stately co-ops or sleek new condos overseen by stiffly collared doormen. But there's a lot more happening on the Upper East Side. Museum Mile throngs with tourists, street artists, and lovers of the arts, drawn to its abundance of high culture. And the eastern side of the neighborhood, toward Yorkville, exhibits a less rarefied character. Second Avenue is home to sports bars, pubs, and some excellent restaurants. A trendy renaissance is in the offing here, sparked by young professionals drawn by some surprisingly good housing prices (for Manhattan). The avenues and commerce-lined thoroughfares can be hectic, but many streets on the Upper East Side are blessedly quiet — just one more way in which this oft-stereotyped neighborhood can be a surprise. Historically, Downtown Brooklyn has been the hub of the borough's municipal activities with many civil service offices and court houses centered around Cadman Plaza, the neighborhood's main hub. Its appeal and vibrancy stem from its housing stock. Handsome Greek revival and Italianate townhouses line the wide, tree-lined streets. These beautiful brick and limestone buildings have long been a mecca for Brooklynites seeking an enclave close to Downtown Brooklyn and lower Manhattan — but far from crowds and highrises. Main drags like Bergen Street, Atlantic Avenue, and Smith Street are peppered with charming boutiques like Collier West in addition to welcoming cafes, bars, and restaurants, including Rucola, French Louie, and Bacchus, to name a few. Fans of new construction will find new condo developments too. Saint Marks Place, The Hendrick, The Boerum, and The Bergen have expanded buyers' opportunities. Renters will also find plenty of options here in a broad range of prices, from the genuinely affordable to the luxurious. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. listing.description:
This beautifully renovated top-floor one-bedroom sublet is located in a full-service, doorman cooperative overlooking Grand Army Plaza. The apartment offers exceptional storage, including abundant closet space and a separate mirrored walk-in closet in the bedroom. Enjoy expansive, sun-filled views of New York Harbor and the Manhattan skyline from both the living room and bedroom. Hardwood floors run throughout the apartment, and just one floor above is a recently renovated roof deck with spectacular 360° views of the harbor, Manhattan, Prospect Park, and even New Jersey and Staten Island in the distance. The building also features a laundry room in the basement. Transportation is exceptionally convenient. The 2 and 3 trains at Grand Army Plaza are just one block away, the D and Q trains are approximately a five-minute walk, and the Long Island Railroad is less than a mile away. The neighborhood offers outstanding amenities, including the popular Saturday Greenmarket at Grand Army Plaza, with the Brooklyn Museum and Brooklyn Botanic Garden about a 10-minute walk from the building. Whole Foods is about one mile away adjacent to the Brooklyn Apple
Store which is about a 20-minute walk. Available for occupancy in September.

From the chaotic, commercial avenues of Nostrand and Utica to the wide, tree-lined esplanades of Eastern Parkway, the streets are always filled with locals shopping, catching up on the corner, and keeping tabs on neighbors. Walk down any of these streets and you're likely to find music playing from idling cars and bright Caribbean flags hanging from windows of apartment buildings. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Its appeal and vibrancy stem from its housing stock. Handsome Greek revival and Italianate townhouses line the wide, tree-lined streets. These beautiful brick and limestone buildings have long been a mecca for Brooklynites seeking an enclave close to Downtown Brooklyn and lower Manhattan — but far from crowds and highrises. Main drags like Bergen Street, Atlantic Avenue, and Smith Street are peppered with charming boutiques like Collier West in addition to welcoming cafes, bars, and restaurants, including Rucola, French Louie, and Bacchus, to name a few. Fans of new construction will find new condo developments too. Saint Marks Place, The Hendrick, The Boerum, and The Bergen have expanded buyers' opportunities. Renters will also find plenty of options here in a broad range of prices, from the genuinely affordable to the luxurious. listing.bodyText: Skip main navigation Search NYC Apartments Reads Search NYC Apartments Good Deals Deal of the Week Most Popular Open Houses Sales Deals Rental Deals Renting NYC Renters' Rights: Resource Hub for Renters NYC Renters' Guide Housing Lotteries Tips and Advice for Renters Buying & Selling Working With a Buyer's Agent: Resource Hub for Buyers First-Time Buyer Guide Buyer Tips and Advice Selling Your Home NYC Life Neighborhood Guides NYC Moving Guide Celebrity Homes Market Data Data Dashboard Market Reports Neighborhood Data Affordability Industry Hub Latest Industry Standards: Resource Hub for Agents Deal of the Week Bright Greenwood studio with in-unit laundry asks $511K By Erika Riley Aug. 11, 2026 In the market for a studio? Sacrificing extra bedrooms in the city can net you some great price tags, without necessarily sacrificing space. If you’re a fan of an open floor plan, take a look at 643 5th Ave. #5C. Our Deal of the Week is a studio in the heart of Greenwood, Brooklyn — a StreetEasy Neighborhood to Watch in 2025 — with tons of natural light and an in-unit washer dryer. 643 5th Ave. #5C Price $511,200 Space Studio, 1 bath Neighborhood Greenwood Borough Brooklyn Learn more about our Deal of the Week! View Listing The price: $511,200 The median asking price for a home in Greenwood was $1.5 million this July, according to the StreetEasy Data Dashboard. That means our Deal of the Week is priced at about a third of the median asking price for the neighborhood! Buyers who put down a 20% down payment of $102,240 can expect to see monthly payments of $3,245. This includes a mortgage payment of $2,607, common charges of $311, and taxes of $327. Monthly prices are even lower than the neighborhood’s median rent, which sat at $3,825 this July. Why you’ll love it… The unit benefits from a wide open floor plan and floor-to-ceiling windows, which keep the space feeling airy and bright. White tile floors throughout also create a sleek and clean vibe. Through a glass-paneled door you’ll find the unit’s private balcony, which faces away from the street. At about 32 square feet, it’s the perfect size for a small patio set where you can enjoy your morning coffee, read a book, or catch up with a friend. The kitchen has a breakfast bar with space for two barstools. Plus, there’s enough room for a small dining table if you prefer to have options. White quartz countertops, white sleek cabinetry, and stainless steel appliances offer a modern look. Appliances include a double-door full-size fridge with freezer drawers, and a full-size oven with a range. There’s even extra cabinetry above the fridge and oven for more storage space. A stacked Bosch washer and dryer are tucked away in the entryway closet, so you won’t have to worry about lugging laundry in and out of the unit. The bathroom, located off the living area, has a similar white and gray color scheme as the rest of the home. It also includes a white floating vanity and soaking tub. To top it all off, the unit has central air conditioning and heat — and very low monthlies. The condo is situated in a 2025-built elevator building with a fitness room and rooftop deck. Commuting to Manhattan is easy with a nearby R stop on Prospect Avenue. The F and G are about a half-mile away. But if you prefer to drive, the building also has a parking garage. Located right off Fifth Avenue, you’ll be surrounded by restaurants, bars and cafes — everything from pizza joints to cocktail bars. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Sales Median asking price 3 beds $2.74M Rentals Median asking base rent 3 beds $7,650 Energetic and inviting, Boerum Hill continues its run as one of New York City's most desirable neighborhoods, all while remaining a secret quietly shared amongst its happy residents. Its appeal and vibrancy stem from its housing stock. Handsome Greek revival and Italianate townhouses line the wide, tree-lined streets. These beautiful brick and limestone buildings have long been a mecca for Brooklynites seeking an enclave close to Downtown Brooklyn and lower Manhattan — but far from crowds and highrises. Main drags like Bergen Street, Atlantic Avenue, and Smith Street are peppered with charming boutiques like Collier West in addition to welcoming cafes, bars, and restaurants, including Rucola, French Louie, and Bacchus, to name a few. Fans of new construction will find new condo developments too. Saint Marks Place, The Hendrick, The Boerum, and The Bergen have expanded buyers' opportunities. Renters will also find plenty of options here in a broad range of prices, from the genuinely affordable to the luxurious. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block. Despite the abundance of seven-figure homes, Cobble Hill has small-town vibe evident in the mom-and-pop stores and Italian influences that dot Court Street. Walk down the sunny commercial strip and you'll pass the local butcher, the baker and the fishmonger — all family-run and equally popular among local residents and foodies from far and wide. Its appeal and vibrancy stem from its housing stock. Handsome Greek revival and Italianate townhouses line the wide, tree-lined streets. These beautiful brick and limestone buildings have long been a mecca for Brooklynites seeking an enclave close to Downtown Brooklyn and lower Manhattan — but far from crowds and highrises. Main drags like Bergen Street, Atlantic Avenue, and Smith Street are peppered with charming boutiques like Collier West in addition to welcoming cafes, bars, and restaurants, including Rucola, French Louie, and Bacchus, to name a few. Fans of new construction will find new condo developments too. Saint Marks Place, The Hendrick, The Boerum, and The Bergen have expanded buyers' opportunities. Renters will also find plenty of options here in a broad range of prices, from the genuinely affordable to the luxurious. Welcome to The Landmark. These homes reflect a contemporary way of life and have been designed to accommodate discerning lifestyles. Building amenities include a doorman and concierge, roof deck with stunning views, residents lounge, and fitness center. Conveniently located near transportation with the R, F and G trains just down the street. Surrounded by restaurants, coffee shops, a farmers market, shopping, nightlife, and even a Whole Foods around the corner! Photos are of a similar unit in the building. 
This apartment can be rented deposit free. Pay a small monthly fee to Rhino, and never pay a security deposit again. Please ask the leasing agent for more information.

Sales Median asking price 1 bed $950K Rentals Median asking base rent 1 bed $4,325 Energetic and inviting, Boerum Hill continues its run as one of New York City's most desirable neighborhoods, all while remaining a secret quietly shared amongst its happy residents. Its appeal and vibrancy stem from its housing stock. Handsome Greek revival and Italianate townhouses line the wide, tree-lined streets. These beautiful brick and limestone buildings have long been a mecca for Brooklynites seeking an enclave close to Downtown Brooklyn and lower Manhattan — but far from crowds and highrises. Main drags like Bergen Street, Atlantic Avenue, and Smith Street are peppered with charming boutiques like Collier West in addition to welcoming cafes, bars, and restaurants, including Rucola, French Louie, and Bacchus, to name a few. Fans of new construction will find new condo developments too. Saint Marks Place, The Hendrick, The Boerum, and The Bergen have expanded buyers' opportunities. Renters will also find plenty of options here in a broad range of prices, from the genuinely affordable to the luxurious. Located near shops, dining, and public transportation, this apartment offers easy access to everything you need.

Despite the abundance of seven-figure homes, Cobble Hill has small-town vibe evident in the mom-and-pop stores and Italian influences that dot Court Street. Walk down the sunny commercial strip and you'll pass the local butcher, the baker and the fishmonger — all family-run and equally popular among local residents and foodies from far and wide. Energetic and inviting, Boerum Hill continues its run as one of New York City's most desirable neighborhoods, all while remaining a secret quietly shared amongst its happy residents. Its appeal and vibrancy stem from its housing stock. Handsome Greek revival and Italianate townhouses line the wide, tree-lined streets. These beautiful brick and limestone buildings have long been a mecca for Brooklynites seeking an enclave close to Downtown Brooklyn and lower Manhattan — but far from crowds and highrises. Main drags like Bergen Street, Atlantic Avenue, and Smith Street are peppered with charming boutiques like Collier West in addition to welcoming cafes, bars, and restaurants, including Rucola, French Louie, and Bacchus, to name a few. Fans of new construction will find new condo developments too. Saint Marks Place, The Hendrick, The Boerum, and The Bergen have expanded buyers' opportunities. Renters will also find plenty of options here in a broad range of prices, from the genuinely affordable to the luxurious. Easy subway access and abundant inventory have drawn many to the area looking for luxury rentals and condos in the area's numerous new apartment towers. Historically, Downtown Brooklyn has been the hub of the borough's municipal activities with many civil service offices and court houses centered around Cadman Plaza, the neighborhood's main hub. With tons of city employees, lawyers and Brooklynites of all types constantly bustling about, Downtown Brooklyn has a decidedly hectic vibe. This, coupled with the area's lack of green space, makes Downtown Brooklyn most appealing to those who can embrace one of Brooklyn's busiest and most trafficked neighborhoods. listing.description: Introducing residence 1401 at 180 Ashland Place, a newly available one-bedroom in the heart of Fort Greene, Brooklyn. This bright and spacious corner unit offers a sweeping open layout, complemented by multiple closets and stunning north-facing city views featuring floor to ceiling windows. The modern oak wood flooring adds a touch of elegance, while the Bertazzoni stainless steel appliances and quartz countertops and backsplash elevate the kitchen's functionality and style. The convenience of an in-home washer and dryer, along with USB/USBC outlets and solar shades, enhances the living experience. The spa-like bathroom is a sanctuary, featuring porcelain tile flooring, light-up vanity mirrors, Grohe fixtures, a medicine cabinet, and a quartz vanity with custom shelving. Located in The Everly, residents enjoy access to two floors of exclusive amenities. The 2nd Floor Clubhouse includes a state-of-the-art fitness center, Flow Studio, Ski Simulator Lodge, The Range Multisport Simulator, The Workshop, Kid's Nook, Content Studio, Fireside Lounge, and a Game Den with billiards, ping-pong, and shuffleboard. Outdoor enthusiasts will appreciate the Great Lawn with a movie screen, terrace with BBQ grills, and a pet run/play area. The 50th Floor Sky Lounge offers an outdoor pool deck with a hot tub, a Serenity Suite with a steam room, The Reserve wine and party room, a Workspace Garden, and a Game Loft with bocce and foosball. The Overlook Lounge provides breathtaking views of Manhattan and Brooklyn. Positioned in vibrant Fort Greene, The Everly places you moments away from Brooklyn's finest attractions including the Barclays Center, and a short subway ride from Manhattan, with convenient access to multiple subway lines, stations and the LIRR. Experience the perfect blend of luxury and location at residence 1401 in The Everly. Amenities: $150/month & Pets: $40/month.

Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. Its appeal and vibrancy stem from its housing stock. Handsome Greek revival and Italianate townhouses line the wide, tree-lined streets. These beautiful brick and limestone buildings have long been a mecca for Brooklynites seeking an enclave close to Downtown Brooklyn and lower Manhattan — but far from crowds and highrises. Main drags like Bergen Street, Atlantic Avenue, and Smith Street are peppered with charming boutiques like Collier West in addition to welcoming cafes, bars, and restaurants, including Rucola, French Louie, and Bacchus, to name a few. Fans of new construction will find new condo developments too. Saint Marks Place, The Hendrick, The Boerum, and The Bergen have expanded buyers' opportunities. Renters will also find plenty of options here in a broad range of prices, from the genuinely affordable to the luxurious. This bright one bedroom residence at Boerum Heights Condominium offers a private balcony, open city views, and full service amenities in the heart of Boerum Hill.

Hardwood floors run throughout, and the open kitchen features light green cabinetry, stainless steel appliances including a Bosch dishwasher, generous counter space, and a breakfast bar with seating.

The bedroom is generously proportioned with large windows and excellent storage, including a walk in closet with built in shelving and hanging space. The marble bathroom is conveniently accessible from both the bedroom and hallway and features a glass enclosed tub and shower, modern vanity, and additional storage. The apartment also offers central air conditioning and an in unit washer and dryer.

Boerum Heights Condominium is a full service elevator building with a full time doorman and concierge, fitness center, common courtyard, live in superintendent, and on site parking.

Located in Boerum Hill and close to Downtown Brooklyn, Fort Greene, and Park Slope, the building offers easy access to dining, shopping, culture, and transportation. Neighborhood favorites include Rucola, French Louie, Sottocasa Pizzeria, Mia's Bakery, Yafa Cafe, Center for Fiction, and Books Are Magic, with Barclays Center, Atlantic Terminal, BAM, Whole Foods, and Trader Joe's all nearby.

Transportation is exceptionally convenient, with the 2, 3, 4, 5, B, D, N, Q, and R subway lines at Atlantic Avenue Barclays Center, along with LIRR service at Atlantic Terminal.

Please note: Pets are on a case by case basis

Sales Median asking price 1 bed $899K Rentals Median asking base rent 1 bed $4,650 Bisected by Flatbush Avenue and bordered by the BQE, Downtown Brooklyn is a rapidly expanding residential neighborhood. Easy subway access and abundant inventory have drawn many to the area looking for luxury rentals and condos in the area's numerous new apartment towers. Historically, Downtown Brooklyn has been the hub of the borough's municipal activities with many civil service offices and court houses centered around Cadman Plaza, the neighborhood's main hub. With tons of city employees, lawyers and Brooklynites of all types constantly bustling about, Downtown Brooklyn has a decidedly hectic vibe. This, coupled with the area's lack of green space, makes Downtown Brooklyn most appealing to those who can embrace one of Brooklyn's busiest and most trafficked neighborhoods. Sales Median asking price 1 bed $899K Rentals Median asking base rent 1 bed $4,650 Bisected by Flatbush Avenue and bordered by the BQE, Downtown Brooklyn is a rapidly expanding residential neighborhood. Easy subway access and abundant inventory have drawn many to the area looking for luxury rentals and condos in the area's numerous new apartment towers. Historically, Downtown Brooklyn has been the hub of the borough's municipal activities with many civil service offices and court houses centered around Cadman Plaza, the neighborhood's main hub. With tons of city employees, lawyers and Brooklynites of all types constantly bustling about, Downtown Brooklyn has a decidedly hectic vibe. This, coupled with the area's lack of green space, makes Downtown Brooklyn most appealing to those who can embrace one of Brooklyn's busiest and most trafficked neighborhoods. Between then and now, Yorkville has seen a lot of change. Tony mansions and elevated trains went up at the turn of the century and then came down in the postwar years as a middle-class population moved in. Now, the neighborhood is a haven of high-rise co-ops and condos interspersed with quiet rows of townhouses. The mixed housing stock makes Yorkville a practical choice for anyone seeking a slowed-down Manhattan vibe. Several avenues over from the throngs of Lexington and Third Avenues, Yorkville maintains a low-key, no-frills feel — it's a place where you'll find more diners and donut shops than upscale lounges and boutiques. This homey attitude is writ in its storefronts, where the food is kept simple and the owners are often from around the block.
